title: FPGA Digital Alarm Clock
summary: A 24-hour alarm clock on an FPGA that keeps steady time from a 50 MHz board clock and counts every button press exactly once.
specs: CORE: Cyclone V FPGA · LANG: VHDL · TEAM: 2
content:
ENSC 252 course project · Simon Fraser University · Team of 2 (with Sumair Amrala)

View more details on GitHub →

The Problem

Building a clock with no processor, operating system or libraries means making every part from logic: turning a 50 MHz board signal into exactly one tick per second, and reading mechanical buttons that bounce, so one press can register several times and skip the time ahead.

Result

A working 24-hour alarm clock with three modes (running, set time and alarm set) showing HH:MM:SS on six 7-segment displays. The alarm only fires when it's armed and the time matches.

Left: running mode on the DE10-Standard, with 24-hour time on the six 7-segment displays. Right: the alarm going off at 00:01:00, with the LEDs lit once the armed alarm matches the current time.

What Went Wrong and the Fix

  • Bouncing buttons: fixed with debounced, edge-detected button logic using a two-stage shift register, so each press becomes exactly one clean pulse.

  • Too fast a clock: the 50 MHz signal is divided by a 25-bit counter (÷ 2²⁵) down to a ≈1 Hz tick.

  • Catching bugs before the board: every module was checked with ModelSim testbenches, then tested on the DE10-Standard.

How It Works

An FSM switches between the three modes. Reusable BCD counters (0–59 and 0–23) built from custom D flip-flops keep the time, and a shared control interface links the counter, editing and display logic. Key terms: VHDL, Cyclone V FPGA, FSM, BCD counters, Quartus Prime, ModelSim.
stats: BOARD CLOCK: 50 MHz → 1 Hz · MODES: 3 · DISPLAY: 6 × 7-segment · TEAM: 2

title: AI Posture Detection System
summary: Real-time slouch detection from a webcam, trained on about 1,500 labelled images: 88.5% best test accuracy across 4 models. Greater Vancouver Regional Science Fair finalist.
specs: CV: OpenCV + MediaPipe · LANG: Python · RESULT: Science fair finalist
content:
Independent project · Greater Vancouver Regional Science Fair finalist

The Problem

People who struggle to keep good posture, or already have neck and back problems from it, slouch gradually over long hours at a computer and rarely get feedback in the moment, when fixing it is easiest. This detector needs nothing but the webcam they already have.

Result

A working real-time Good / Poor posture detector that shows its confidence on screen: 88.5% best accuracy on test data and about 60–70% in live webcam use. Finalist at the Greater Vancouver Regional Science Fair.

The detector tested on sample posture photos: good posture (left) and poor posture (right), each with the predicted class and the model’s confidence.

What Went Wrong and the Fix

Across two trials the four models scored between 64% and 88.5% on test data, and their rankings swung a lot: Gradient Boosting dropped from 88.5% to 74.3% while Ridge jumped from 64.2% to 81.6%. In live use the detector was right about 60–70% of the time.

The swings showed the dataset was too small and too uniform for the models to learn posture reliably. The lesson: a model is only as good as how varied its data is. Next time I'd collect samples from more people, camera angles and lighting conditions.

How It Works

MediaPipe extracts body and face landmarks from each webcam frame, the coordinates are saved to a CSV dataset, and four scikit-learn classifiers were trained and compared. Key terms: Python, OpenCV, MediaPipe, Pandas, scikit-learn (Logistic Regression, Ridge, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting), Teachable Machine.

Built on Nicholas Renotte’s Body Language Decoder tutorial.
stats: BEST TEST ACCURACY: 88.5% · TRAINING IMAGES: ~1,500 · LANDMARKS / FRAME: 33 · SCIENCE FAIR: Finalist

title: Automatic Blueberry Sorter
summary: Sorts blueberries by size and automatically rejects anything that isn't a blueberry, using a colour sensor and a servo-driven flap.
category: TCS3200 COLOR SENSOR · SG90 SERVO · ELECTRIC MOTORS
specs: SENSOR: TCS3200 · DRIVE: 12V DC + SG90 servo · ROLE: Project manager (team of 8)
content:
ENSC 100W design lab project · Simon Fraser University · Team of 8

The Problem

Small growers and packers sort blueberries by size and pick out debris and bad berries largely by hand: slow, repetitive work. The goal was a machine that does both, and comes apart for washing between batches.

Result

A motor-driven centrifugal sorter that drops berries into small (8 × 10 mm) and large (18 × 20 mm) slots, sends accepted berries down 3 cm tunnels and catches rejects in a pull-out tray.

Presenting the Blueberry Sorter 9000 with my team of 8 at the ENSC 100W design showcase, Simon Fraser University.

What Went Wrong

The final prototype worked as a proof of concept, sorting by size and flagging off-colour objects, but it wasn't reliable enough to sort consistently. Managing a team of 8 through design, build and integration taught me as much as the hardware did.

How It Works

A TCS3200 colour sensor reads each berry's RGB values from within 10 mm and compares them with a calibrated blueberry range, RGB(25, 35, 105) to RGB(100, 160, 235). Anything outside the range makes an SG90 servo sweep a 30° flap that diverts it into the reject hole. A 12V DC motor with an L298 driver feeds the berries. Key terms: TCS3200, SG90 servo, 12V DC motor, L298 driver, centrifugal sorting.
stats: SIZE CLASSES: 2 · REJECT FLAP: 30° servo · TEAM: 8 · MY ROLE: Project manager

title: Split
summary: Cuts my friend groups' 30-minute "where do we eat?" debates to under 5 minutes, then splits the bill by what each person actually ate.
specs: STACK: HTML, CSS, JavaScript · AI: Gemini + Cloudflare Worker · EVENT: ProtoHacks
content:
ProtoHacks hackathon · Team of 4

Try the app → View the code on GitHub → Devpost →

The Problem

Every time my friends and I eat out, we spend 30+ minutes deciding where to go, someone ends up over budget, and the bill gets split evenly even when one person had a salad and another had a steak and two drinks. Then nobody remembers who owes who.

What It Does

  • Group: everyone enters their budget, cuisine, distance and diet. Split finds real restaurants, ranks them by how many people they work for, and the group votes.

  • Planner: snap the menu, enter the headcount and budget, and get an order that fits after tax and tip.

  • Fair Split: snap the receipt, everyone taps what they ate, and tax, tip and discounts are shared by what each person ordered. Payment requests go out by e-Transfer, PayPal or Venmo.

  • Ledger: past meals, who owes who, and how much you've spent.

Result

Choosing a restaurant went from 30+ minutes of back-and-forth to under 5 minutes, because Split ranks real options by how well they fit everyone's budget, cuisine, distance and diet. It's now used across our own friend groups, and the ledger keeps track of exactly who owes who after every meal.

What Went Wrong and the Fix

  • The API key couldn't be kept secret. GitHub Pages only serves files, so the live site was stuck in demo mode. We moved the key to a Cloudflare Worker, so it never reaches the public repo or users' browsers.

  • Four people, one repo. Merge conflicts and overwritten work, so we got much better at stashing, pulling and resolving conflicts.

  • Gemini "high demand" errors. We kept a demo mode with sample data as a backup for the presentation.

How It Works

Gemini reads menus and receipts from photos and searches for restaurants. The fair split gives each person their own food plus a share of tax, tip and discounts in proportion to what they ordered, counted in whole cents so the shares always add up to the bill exactly. Key terms: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Google Gemini, Cloudflare Worker, Firebase Realtime Database, GitHub Pages, PWA.
stats: PICKING A PLACE: 30+ → under 5 min · FEATURES: 4 · TEAM: 4 · EVENT: ProtoHacks

title: Animu
summary: Turns your Spotify music into a living backdrop: when an anime song plays, Animu finds the matching opening and loops it full-screen behind the music.
category: JAVASCRIPT · NODE.JS · SPOTIFY API · ANIMETHEMES API
specs: RUNTIME: Node.js · APIs: Spotify + AnimeThemes · TYPE: Personal
content:
Personal project · Built for fun

View the code on GitHub →

The Problem

When I study with music on, my second monitor shows nothing, or a static album cover. I wanted a cleaner study setup where the screen matches what I'm listening to. It's a personal tool I run during study sessions.

Result

Two songs, two openings: the dim slider on the right darkens the video (left) or lets it shine through (right), with now-playing info and playback controls along the bottom.

What Went Wrong and the Fix

  • Songs that don't match an opening directly: Animu uses the track and album info to work out which anime it's from and shows its first opening instead. If that also fails, the song's cover art becomes the background.

  • Videos filling up storage: each opening downloads once and streams while it loads, and the cache stays under 3 GB by removing the least recently watched videos.

  • Bright videos are tiring to look at: a dim slider darkens the video without blurring it.

How It Works

Spotify sign-in uses PKCE (no client secret) to follow the current track and send playback controls back. Matching searches the AnimeThemes catalog by song title and artist credits, with title normalization. I designed the system and built it with AI-assisted coding. Key terms: Node.js, Spotify Web API (PKCE), AnimeThemes API, video caching (LRU).

Disclaimer: Animu is a personal, non-commercial project. Anime openings are streamed from AnimeThemes and belong to their respective copyright holders.
stats: VIDEO CACHE: under 3 GB · APIs: Spotify + AnimeThemes · RUNTIME: Node.js · TYPE: Personal

title: Sakura Assistant
summary: Makes focusing feel rewarding: a 3D anime companion keeps you on task, and focus sessions and finished tasks earn unlocks.
specs: BACKEND: Python (FastAPI) · AI: Gemini + ElevenLabs · EVENT: StormHacks 2026
content:
StormHacks 2026 hackathon · Team of 4 · My role: 3D character models and the Python backend

View the code on GitHub → Devpost →

The Problem

Students sit down to study and get pulled away by games, YouTube and social media, and most productivity tools feel too cold to stick with. Sakura makes focus rewarding: a companion keeps you on task, and real work earns unlocks.

Result

A Windows desktop app with nine characters. Petals earned from focus sessions and quests unlock new characters, outfits and backgrounds. Real work unlocks rewards, not real money.

The collection of nine characters (left), and the dressing room where outfits, headwear, eyewear and backgrounds are swapped (right).

What Went Wrong and the Fix

  • Voice replies felt slow: waiting for Gemini's full answer before speaking was too slow, so the backend splits the reply into sentences, sends each one to ElevenLabs as soon as it's ready, and saves every generated line for reuse.

  • Characters drifting out of persona: each character has its own Gemini system prompt, so it stays in character while still taking real actions like adding a quest or scheduling a session.

  • Distractions: in focus mode, opening a blocked app or website costs you petals and the companion closes it.

Start a focus session and the timer runs. Open a blocked app or website and your companion scolds you, takes away petals and closes the distraction.

How It Works

I designed and built the 3D character models in VRoid Studio, and built the Python backend with AI-assisted coding: game rules, rewards, quests, scheduling and the focus watcher. Key terms: Python, FastAPI, Google Gemini, ElevenLabs (English and Japanese voices), VRoid Studio, three.js.

Disclaimer: Sakura Assistant was built only for the hackathon and is not released for public use. Several characters are fan-made recreations of characters from existing anime, and those characters belong to their respective copyright holders.
stats: CHARACTERS: 9 · VOICES: English + Japanese · TEAM: 4 · EVENT: StormHacks 2026
